title: New Grant Will Support Research on Emerging Cold-Hardy Grapevine Disease - University of New Hampshire
content: Cold hardy grapes are the foundation of a thriving $400 million industry that includes wine production and agrotourism and stretches from the northern Midwest to the Great Lakes to the Northeast, including New Hampshire.  According to WineAmerica's 2025 Economic Impact Study, New Hampshire's wine industry supports an estimated 154,500 winery-related visits annually, generating approximately $29.5 million in tourism expenditures and contributing to local economies. However, cold hardy grapes are facing an emerging threat: a grapevine trunk disease caused by a species of fungi in the genus Fusarium. While Fusarium species are well known as pathogens of many crops, their role in cold hardy grapevine trunk disease remains poorly understood. Key questions include where disease-causing populations originate, how and when they invading the grapevines, or how to detect them early enough to inform management decisions. A new research project funded by the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture will investigate an emerging Fusarium-associated disease affecting cold-hardy grapevines. The project, “Exploring Fusarium Trunk Decline, an Emerging Threat to Cold-Hardy Grapevines in the U.S.,” is led by Xiaochen Yuan, assistant professor, and Suzanne Slack, adjunct research faculty, both in the department of agriculture, nutrition, and food systems. The project builds on several years of research by Yuan and Slack investigating the role of Fusarium species in grapevine decline in northern U.S. production regions. Previous vineyard surveys recovered Fusarium species from declining grapevines, and pathogenicity studies demonstrated that some of these isolates can cause disease in both cold-hardy hybrid and Vitis vinifera grape cultivars. Substantial yield losses have also been documented in vineyards affected by decline, highlighting the need to better understand the biology, distribution, and management of this emerging disease. The new project will expand this work across the Midwest, Great Lakes, and Northeast to determine the geographic distribution and genetic diversity of Fusarium populations associated with grapevine trunk disease, evaluate their ability to cause disease and mycotoxigenic potential, improve diagnostic approaches, and investigate factors that may influence disease development and management. “An important part is figuring out how widespread this problem actually is,” says Slack. “We have data from the Midwest, but since we've been here [in New Hampshire], we've already been in contact with local vineyards having this problem, and we did find Fusarium inside their samples.” The goal is to provide grape growers with practical tools for earlier disease recognition and science-based management recommendations that can reduce disease losses and protect vineyard productivity. “Right now, it takes almost two months to determine if it's the correct Fusarium. There are some species that are non-pathogenic that could be in the wood,” says Slack. “So we need to test if it's the one that's pathogenic or the strains that are just kind of hanging out. We want to develop a quick way to tell a grower, ‘Yes, it's here,’ so they can make quick management decisions.” “We won't say we'll completely eliminate it, but at least we can help our growers to manage it,” adds Yuan. The project also represents an important collaboration among UNH researchers, USDA-ARS scientist Kristi Gdanetz MacCready, Extension specialists, diagnostic laboratories, and grape growers across the region. Results will be shared with growers and industry professionals through Extension programming, publications, diagnostic resources, and regional outreach. title: What a UNH professor taught me about politics, disagreement and hate: Splaine - Seacoastonline.com
content: While a sophomore at the University of New Hampshire in 1967, I signed up for American History 101, taught by Professor David Long. Many UNH students remember him as a popular teacher with a booming, pleasant voice that made his lectures both fascinating and enjoyable. His classes incorporated his textbook, titled "The American Story" (McGraw-Hill, 1955) with tidbits of yarns he would tell us, almost like a casual chat. Instead of just dates and names, he put context into his lectures that encouraged an understanding of the year-to-year, decade-to-decade evolution of American history, along with the "why" of our history − good and bad − the tragic, as well as the human progress. His course led me to major in history, leading to my formal certification to teach high school history upon graduation.  Incidentally, my brother John also had his class.  He was one of our favorites. I remember that Professor Long's lessons taught that as our American experience evolves, the daily issues that challenge us need not divide us as human beings. Too often we hate one another just because we have differences of opinion. Opinion need not cause hate. I thought of Dr. Long during the past few weeks as I felt an inner tension about the pending Nov. 3 election. I know friends felt the same nervousness. Much was at stake, regardless of your party affiliation. Uncertainty is always tense. I watched many television news and news talk shows these past few weeks. I intentionally ignored social media and instead focused on a diversity of news, seeking to hear about varied ideas people had, their points of view, their fears about election security, and their concerns about voter intimidation. I tried to absorb the rhetoric of the candidates. I noticed that all candidates made things up at times, some more than others, and just about all candidates exaggerated the wrongdoings of their opponents. Such is electioneering − it happens everywhere, and likely goes back to the days of old Rome and Greece. The 2026 midterms are over, and two years − just 104 weeks − will pass, and those who don't support last Tuesday's results will soon have another day. During that time, wouldn't it be good for all of us to accept Professor Long's view of the American story and appreciate that we can each differ with one another. That's okay. That's politics. Everyone has an opinion. Yes, there are important issues about which we differ. But even the life and death issues will change over time and hating one another doesn't improve our efforts to find answers.  We can be passionate about our positions on issues without hating one another to the point of violence, or of not even trying to talk with one another. We need leaders who will work together to resolve our commonality, work toward our common good, reject greed and the "me-first" or "me-only" philosophy, and find ways of friendship and peace. If all that sounds like a lecture, credit it to a wonderful late UNH professor named David Long. Our Republican and Democratic leaders, with their varying philosophies, will be going to our State House in coming weeks, or traveling to assume their duties in Washington. Let them be passionate, and fight for their causes. But let's hope they put their energies into positive accomplishments for us.  And let's hope they can do that job together. Observation:  I'm impressed that Texas U.S. Senator-elect James Talarico speaks of love, and isn't ashamed of it. Today's quote. "Regardless of individual beliefs, which we all respect of each other, it is amazing to think about all of the voting locations across the state and the country where folks just like you volunteer to ensure fair elections are executed with accuracy, efficiency, transparency, and friendliness."  - Brian Gibb, Ward 1 Moderator in a note to his poll volunteers who worked into the night on Tuesday.  Let's thank them for protecting our democracy. Variously since 1969, Jim Splaine has been New Hampshire state senator for six years and state representative for 24 years.  He was six-term Portsmouth Assistant Mayor for 12 years, nine-term city councilor for 18 years, elected as Police Commissioner, and served on the School Board.  jimsplaineportsmouthNH@gmail.com

BOSTON (WHDH) - Andy Smith, Director of the UNH Survey Center, said his polling showed that the midterms were a referendum on President Trump. Smith said motivated democrats showed up at the polls and helped drive the results. “It was a question if those people who are least likely to vote, younger voters, they are the ones who are driving the energy, in the democratic party, it appears they turned out and voted,” Smith said. This was evident in the Senate race in New Hampshire, where democrat Chris Pappas beat republican John Sununu. “Among Sununu supporters, about 60 percent had nothing to do with Trump, but among Pappas supporters, 87% said their vote was a vote against Donald Trump,” Smith said. Smith said that motivation carried down the ballot. Voters often choose candidates from the same party once they enter the voting booth. “They typically vote straight ticket; the party that gets them to the polls in the first place, they are going to vote for that party all the way down the line,” Smith said. Smith said republicans will now have to decide what comes next. “They have to decide if [it is] Trump’s party or a more ideologically conservative republican,” Smith said. title: Voices of UNH Manchester Wildcats Series: Meet Mechanical Engineering Technology Major, Kieran McCurdy, '25 - University of New Hampshire
content: Are you considering a future in mechanical engineering technology? Meet Kieran McCurdy, class of '25 at UNH Manchester, whose journey offers a firsthand look at the value of this dynamic program. Whether you’re a prospective student or simply curious about what makes UNH Manchester stand out, Kieran’s experience highlights the unique opportunities, hands-on learning, and career advantages waiting for you. For Kieran, the decision to attend UNH Manchester was driven by the program’s practical focus and its strong industry connections. He shares, “UNH Manchester is a hub for all these different companies. When you graduate, there are all these job opportunities that you can go into.” The campus’s location in the heart of Manchester, NH, puts students close to leading engineering firms and tech companies, opening doors to internships, networking, and career placement right after graduation. Kieran’s experience in the mechanical engineering technology program is marked by a diverse curriculum and hands-on learning. He explains, “My favorite thing about the mechanical engineering technology program at UNH Manchester is the array of classes you take. title: The Democracy Summit: UNH’s Democracy Infosession - The New Hampshire
content: On Wednesday Oct. 7, the Responsible Governance and Sustainable Citizenship Project (RGSCP) hosted The University of New Hampshire’s (UNH) Democracy Summit. This is RGSCP’s first event for the fall semester, in which they will be answering questions like “What does democracy mean?” and, “Is the concept of democratic governance in jeopardy?” The wide range of faculty in attendance offered many topics for students, as well as the community, to hear about throughout the entirety of Wednesday. The Democracy Summit organized by the RGSCP held many seminars to educate the public about civics. The summit saw college students, high school students, other faculty, and many more. The overall outcome of the summit was considered a success and works to pave the way for more events throughout the school year. Alynna Lyon, professor of Political Violence and International Affairs at UNH, spoke on “Can Democracy Create Peace?” In her section, Lyon covered what constitutes a democracy, as well as how it creates peace between countries. A pair of democracies do not make war. The more democratic two countries are, the less their chance of mutual violence. Lyon touched on the Kantian Triangle, a framework for causes of peace linking democracy, economic interdependence, and membership in international organizations. The triangle was created by Immanuel Kant in his essay “Perceptual Peace” which proposed elements and conditions for lasting peace throughout many countries. With high levels in the Kantian Triangle elements, the incidence of fatal disputes drops by 95%. “We are seeing declining levels of democracy throughout the globe,” said Lyon. Components of democracy include regular elections for the most powerful government positions, near universal franchise meaning the right to vote, secret balloting, civil liberties and political rights, such as free press and free speech, and competitive political parties; not everybody wins all the time. Lyon’s talk included many statistics and research about democracy, violence, as well as the differing tactics that have been taken to promote democracy in other countries. Through this research, Lyon argued that democracy is good for human beings. Aspects correlated with democracy such as literacy rate, education levels, income levels, and life expectancy all increase in democratic states. “Democracies are going down, violence at the international level is going up,” said Professor Lyon. Another section focused on The New Hampshire Declaration of Independence with Sue Siggelakis, a professor of Political Science and Justice Studies at theUNH. Siggelakis spoke about how John Adams and his associates worked together to create pressure on the people in the Continental Congress to cause action. From there, the declaration encouraged independence. Siggelakis helped break down the language and how the writers emulated a lot of the British style of diction. Siggelakis also emphasized the organization, and how this gives insight into what the writers were feeling about the current conflicts within the states. The New Hampshire Declaration of Independence states themselves free and independent, and exemplifies the British syntax such as “whereas” within the text, as well as following along with the other colonies. “And Whereas We of this Colony of New Hampshire have the Example of several of the most Respectable of our Sister Colonies before us for Entering upon that most Important Step of a Disunion from Great Britain, and Declaring ourselves FREE and INDEPENDENT of the Crown thereof…” Another chunk of the Declaration says, “WE DO, therefore Declare that it is the opinion of this Assembly that our Delegates at the Continental Congress should be instructed, and they are hereby Instructed to join with the other Colonies in Declaring THE THIRTEEN UNITED COLONIES, A FREE AND INDEPENDENT STATE…” Here we see the call to action that  Siggelakis referred to that the colonies were pushing the Congress towards. Another section of the Democracy Summit was led by James Wible, a professor of economics at UNH. “Ten Remarkable Economic Features of the U.S. Constitution” focused on parts of the U.S. Constitution that set up our country for its current economic standpoint. Professor Wible included honorable mentions such as: importation of slaves could be banned after 1808, no compensation was given to slave owners upon freeing of the slaves, the eighteenth amendment instating the Prohibition then repealed by the twenty-first amendment. A few of the features Professor Wible included are: The RGSCP recently voted towards making civics a part of the discovery curriculum at UNH, furthering the education of the student body. The Democracy Summit by the RGSCP was a step in presenting civics education to those within the community.

title: UNH English professor emeritus Andy Merton releases new autobiography - The New Hampshire
content: On Thursday Nov. 5 at 5pm, former University of New Hampshire (UNH) English professor Andy Merton is set to read passages from his new autobiography, Gloria Steinem Blurbed Me (And Other Miracles). The reading, located in Hamilton Smith Hall, brings Merton back to the place he taught writing for more than forty years. Throughout his decades at UNH, Merton taught courses ranging in subject matter from creative nonfiction, to travel writing, to advanced essay writing—all to both undergraduate and graduate students—but his main passion and role in the English Department was as a leading professor in journalism. Five years after beginning his professional career in the world of journalism through his work with various daily newspapers, such as The Gloucester Daily Times and the Boston Herald Traveler, Merton was hired by UNH to teach about the craft. However, his story at the school didn’t begin there. Merton studied as an undergraduate at UNH—graduating in 1967 with a Bachelor of Arts in History, alongside a minor in Psychology. He recollects in our interview: “ I studied journalism with the only journalist on the faculty at that time, Don Murray.” He goes on to say that, as a professor years down the line, he worked with Murray to expand course offerings, helping to pave the way for the richly diverse English Department the university is proud of today. Between 2008-2014, Merton was the chair of UNH’s English Department. During his forty-three years as an integral part of the school’s faculty, Merton’s love of writing not only blossomed, but expanded into new territory, thanks in part to the “influences of [his] English Department poet colleagues, Charles Simic and Mekeel McBride.” In 1985, Merton’s affinity for the genre deepened, eventually making its way into both his creative writing and coursework. Merton would go on to have four of his poetry books published and an opportunity to teach poetry writing workshops in his last few years as an English professor. Poetry and journalism acted as guiding forces in Merton’s life, culminating in his autobiography, Gloria Steinem Blurbed Me (And Other Miracles), which hit shelves this past summer. Merton details how the book came together. He claims that it was “not the book [he] started out to write,” an original vision he described to be a memoir “purely about [his] women’s rights and gay rights activism,” but through writing and continually getting off track telling “other stories,” the book flourished into something else entirely. His “memoir became [his] autobiography.” From his early childhood in a Jewish family following WWII, to his college days at UNH (which, in fact, includes his writing for The New Hampshire), to his writing career as a professor, journalist and, eventually, a poet, “Gloria covers most of [Merton’s] life.” In many respects, the form of his work directly relates to his story, in that he “uses poetry as part of the narrative,” a facet of the book he ensured would be accessible enough so that readers who may not be familiar with much poetry, or perhaps simply don’t enjoy it, can engage with the novel in meaningful ways. “The poems are designed to move the text along,” Merton explains. In broad ways, Gloria was a synthesis of Merton’s professional and creative life. It’s a story steeped in realism that is told, in part, with poetry. Merton mentioned that his process for writing the book balanced his journalistic intuitions with those of poetry and creative writing. Being used to rigid deadlines in the world of journalism, Merton made sure to write “200 words a day,” a self-imposed rule that he made sure his editor enforced. Still, his expedition in lifelong reflection was a joyous one—full of memories, conversations with friends, digging through archived published work, and “small ‘oh, yeah!’ moments almost every day.” Gloria Steinem Blurbed Me (And Other Miracles) was published on Aug. 15 by Accents Publishing, a small, independent press that mostly publishes poetry books—including some of Merton’s own. It’s a book that celebrates a life in pursuit of what the author truly loves: the craft of writing and the transferral of that craft to the next generations of writers. “My career at UNH was a dream job, allowing me to combine teaching—which I thoroughly enjoyed—with my writing,” he proudly says. Following a few months’ worth of readings and occasional podcast appearances, Merton is returning to UNH to read passages from his autobiography. The reading will take place in Hamilton Smith Hall on Thursday, Nov. 5 at 5pm—showcasing a writer with a deep devotion to the art, speaking in the very place that inspired him for more than four decades. Alex Hankins is a writer who covers stories ranging from the arts to updates within UNH's English Department. He is a graduate student in UNH's English MFA program, and received his undergraduate degree at here at UNH as well. Alex also serves as the editor for contributor writers in The New Hampshire.

title: Turning Point USA at UNH hosts a 'Pick Up the Mic' with Jack Posobiec - The New Hampshire
content: On Thursday, Oct. 22 Turning Point USA (TPUSA) hosted a surprise Pick Up The Mic event at the University of New Hampshire (UNH) featuring right-wing political figure Jack Posobiec, popular on the social media platform X, debating abortion rights, foreign policy, religion and more with students. The event was located on the Great Lawn from 11:00 AM to 12:00 PM and attracted around 200 attendees. Among the organizers were Caleb Brower, sophomore and chapter president of TPUSA at UNH. Brower expressed that the event was much more successful than anyone had anticipated, considering the lack of political activity at UNH and the size of the Chapter on-campus. Brower’s only critique was the majority of the attendee’s preaching to the choir. “Unfortunately most people agreed,” said Brower. These attendees explained that they did not feel comfortable speaking on their political views in class and expressed gratitude towards the event. There were one or two people that were not interested in civil discourse and approached with hostility. “They start yelling ‘you shouldn't be here.’” Posebiec said during an interview. “And it seemed to me though that they seem to think that if you have a conversation about something where people disagree, that even the civil exhibit of that is somehow problematic.” Brower similarly criticized these interactions as they only produced “one-liners” trying to win the last word instead of productive debates. Brower recalled that foreign policy was the most touched on subject and was surprised by its popularity. Specifically, the concerns were centered around tensions in the Middle East, including the U.S.’s close relationship with Israel. Folks that were left-leaning argued that the “U.S. should not be funding a genocide,” primarily referring to the war in Gaza. Additionally, right-leaning participants dissented the U.S.’s involvement with foreign countries saying that sending resources that are not mutually beneficial is not putting America first. Brower then highlighted the last question from an attendee asking about the truth of Charlie Kirk’s assassination in Sept. 2025, in light of recent theories on social media that the assasination was a conspiracy by Israel. Posobiec denied these accusations and claimed he was certain the assassination was not a larger conspiracy. No matter how controversial or problematic the question may be, Turning Point’s doctrine is committed to defending the right to free speech. Brower admired this dedication to free speech as members from Turning Point’s Headquarters in Phoenix, AZ allowed the attendee to ask questions regarding Kirk’s assassination despite already being out of time. The TPUSA Chapter at UNH has been on more people's radars than last year thanks to events such as Pick Up The Mic. Most of the executive team from previous years stepped down, leading to Brower stepping up as president and taking agency in this role. “[The chapter] Really didn't exist in a meaningful way beforehand,” said Brower. Brower ran into a learning curve as he ambitiously took on a leading role without guidance. A main challenge was not becoming a “repeat” of the republican party club at UNH. To combat this, Brower focused on events rather than weekly meetings with the TPUSA chapter. During UNH’s Parents Weekend on Oct. 17, TPUSA’s chapter set up their own tailgate with free food, games and invited local republican politicians. Brower said this was “certainly the move” as just these two events have attracted great success for TPUSA at UNH. Brower’s motivation is relentless despite UNH’s lack of political presence. TPUSA plans to host at least one more major event this semester and Brower wants to make sure it is memorable. The struggle Brower faces is choosing from a TPUSA’s list of political figures, as many are irrelevant to the average person. “We’re gonna go all out and get someone who [people] actually care about,” said Brower. title: UNH students, faculty oppose potential removal of up to 300k books from library - New Hampshire Public Radio
content: Justin Kostopulos is not a traditional art history student at UNH. He’s 35 and a commuter, so he spends a lot of his time between classes wandering the stacks of the library. When he found out the Dimond Library was reviewing nearly 300,000 print titles for potential removal, he started a petition to ask the university to reconsider. Within a week, it gathered over 600 signatures. “Removing these texts, I think, erases decades of accrued wisdom and insight,” he said. “It deprives students the unique experience of just handling a physical book, which many times can spark curiosity and critical thinking in ways that digital media often cannot.” The book review is part of an effort by UNH to modernize its library, which was last renovated in 1996. UNH said in internal communications to staff and students that was shared with NHPR that the school was a decade overdue in going through their collections. UNH is also planning to open a new student center in the library’s unused space in a few years. UNH said their library is prioritizing digital collections to serve online students, but Kostopulos said there’s still a lot of value to keeping physical copies. “After speaking with many of my peers since starting this petition,” he said. “Many students, myself included, retain information better through physical books rather than reading something online.” The university gave faculty six weeks to review the list of potential titles, ending on Oct. 21. But some faculty, including UNH History Professor Eliga Gould, said that wasn’t enough time. As a historian, Gould also said that interests and access to technology often change, and it’s valuable to keep books, especially older ones. “There is also no guarantee that books now available in online databases always will be there,” he said. “Some of the books slated for removal are over 100 years old. Will a pdf still be here in another 100 years? Today's best practice is all too often tomorrow's regret.” He also recalled what some faculty members jokingly called “dumpstergate,” when thousands of books from the Dimond Library were found in a dumpster in 2014. Even though the online collections may be more convenient, Gould said there is value to keeping print books, especially in a public university, since online books are not accessible to a general public that doesn’t have login to large online collections like HathiTrust. “It's hugely important to have those print books available,” he said. “We're a public institution. This is open to the general public and that's a huge part of our mission as a land grant university.” The university is still planning on moving forward with the renovation, but released a FAQ internally to address concerns. The FAQ said the books were selected for review because they hadn’t been checked out in over a decade, and are easily found in another library, or online. “We default to purchasing electronic books rather than print books. We don’t have the budget to purchase more than one copy of a book, so the collection growth is all electronic and has been for the last ten years, since we adopted an e-preferred policy,” the FAQ said. “The print books we own are an increasingly aging and increasingly smaller percentage of our overall collection.” The university is currently reviewing the feedback from faculty, according to the FAQ shared with staff and students. title: UNH Students Nominated for Marshall, Rhodes Scholarships - University of New Hampshire
content: UNH students Will Steere ’27 and Eben Quenneville ’27 were nominated for 2026 Marshall scholarships, with Quenneville also earning an endorsement for a 2026 Rhodes scholarship. Marshall and Rhodes scholarships are two of the most prestigious and competitive awards available to U.S. students. Steere learned this week that he is a finalist for the Marshall opportunity and will have an interview upcoming. Quenneville was not selected as a finalist for either honor. The Rhodes scholarship provides support for students to study at the University of Oxford and is the “oldest and most celebrated” international postgraduate award, according to the Rhodes website. Marshall scholarships offer 1-to-3 years of post-graduate study to students pursuing a graduate degree in the United Kingdom. Recipients can study in virtually any field at a UK institution of their choice. “Being nominated by UNH for the Marshall Scholarship is an exciting recognition for progressing toward this national award. It feels special to have passed the interview process and earned a nomination by UNH, and I am hopeful that I can win this scholarship and bring recognition to UNH and CEPS,” Steere says. Adds Quenneville: “It's an extraordinary privilege to have so many wonderful mentors at UNH and beyond. When I arrived at UNH, I certainly wasn't imagining that I would one day be applying for scholarships like the Rhodes and Marshall. But over the past few years, I've had opportunities to contribute to exciting scientific research, help launch a satellite, work with researchers around the world, and make a meaningful difference in physics education on campus. Those experiences, and the encouragement of the people I've worked with, have given me the confidence to pursue opportunities that once seemed out of reach.” Steere, a chemical engineering honors student, earned first place for his presentation on catalytic biomass valorization research at UNH’s Undergraduate Research Conference during his junior year, an achievement he includes among his proudest as a student. He also earned an internship at the National Laboratory of the Rockies in Golden, Colorado, which he described as “one of the most impactful experiences I have had.” “I connected with top researchers in my field and learned about the operations of the US Department of Energy, but I also led a high-level research project tied to the Genesis mission aiming to make progress toward AI-driven research laboratories for catalysis,” Steere says. Steere hopes to earn a Ph.D. in chemical engineering “to transfer my research in catalysis into impactful commercial processes.” He is interested in founding a startup based off the catalytic technology he plans to develop during his Ph.D. work or in joining a research institute like a national laboratory in the United States or somewhere global. Quenneville, an engineering physics honors student, counts his work improving physics education for other students at UNH among his proudest achievements since arriving on campus. He has been involved in the Physics Learning Assistant program since his first semester, an offering that places undergraduates in introductory physics classrooms to help their peers work through problems and overcome conceptual hurdles, he says. “It’s tremendously rewarding to help other students develop their understanding of physics,” Quenneville says. “Teaching also forces you to understand the material more deeply yourself, and I think that experience has been invaluable to my own success in research and advanced coursework.” He has also worked with Alec Mercer ’26 and Benjamin Chandran, professor in the College of Engineering and Physical Sciences, to overhaul UNH’s physics tutoring center, now known as the Physics Assistance and Resource Center (PARC). Quenneville has pursued a variety of research as a student (he earned the Barry Goldwater scholarship in recognition of that research), most recently partnering with Chandran and Jonathan Squire from the University of Otago in New Zealand to better understand solar wind. He also helped develop and launch 3UCubed, a satellite “about the size of a loaf of bread” that was part of NASA’s IMAP student collaboration. Quenneville’s career goal is to become a professor of plasma physics, a pursuit “that would allow me to combine my two great interests: teaching and research.” He credited the “wonderful people” at UNH’s Office of National Fellowships, who have played a key role in facilitating the Marshall and Rhodes opportunities as well as a host of others throughout his time at UNH, including the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship and a Fulbright. title: UNH Hosts New England’s First Aerospace Industry Expo - University of New Hampshire
content: New England’s aerospace industry took center stage at the University of New Hampshire on October 28 and 29 as the university hosted the region’s first comprehensive space-focused expo, bringing together innovators, researchers, manufacturers, government leaders and the next generation of talent for two days of discovery, collaboration and inspiration. Presented in partnership with the N.H. Department of Business and Economic Affairs (BEA) and the NH Aerospace & Defense Consortium (NHADC), the inaugural Northeast Space, Technology, Trade, and Research Expo (NE STTAR Expo) transformed UNH’s Memorial Union Building into a hub of cutting-edge technology, groundbreaking research, and industry engagement. More than 700 attendees learned about emerging technologies, research innovations and workforce opportunities across aerospace, autonomous systems, propulsion, advanced manufacturing, and materials science. “The aerospace industry is vital to New Hampshire’s economy, supporting good-paying jobs and businesses across the Granite State as our leading export industry,” said U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who attended the event. “It is thanks to everyone who joined us at the inaugural NE STTAR Expo, especially the University of New Hampshire, the New Hampshire Department of Business and Economic Affairs and the New Hampshire Aerospace & Defense Consortium, for the partnerships you all foster between industry, academia and government to ensure we remain on the cutting-edge and a global leader.” The Expo featured 64 exhibitors, including 50 businesses and 14 university and partner organizations. Approximately 450 industry professionals, exhibitors and other attendees participated, along with 175 students in grades 8-12 and 80 UNH students. The Expo also offered tours of the Space Science Center in Morse Hall and the John Olson Advanced Manufacturing Center throughout both days. The event highlighted the growing importance of New Hampshire’s aerospace and defense sector, which includes roughly 300 companies, employs more than 10,500 people, and generates an estimated $7.5 billion in economic output statewide. As a national leader in space research, UNH provided a fitting venue for the event. The university’s work spans mission leadership, instrument development, data analysis, and simulation, with research ranging from Earth’s upper atmosphere to the farthest reaches of the universe. The first day focused on industry engagement through keynote presentations, technology demonstrations, exhibits, and networking opportunities. The second day shifted attention to workforce development, connecting students with professionals through a career fair, educational programming, and campus facility tours. The inaugural expo underscored New Hampshire’s growing role in the aerospace and space economy while fostering partnerships that will help drive future innovation and workforce development. “As we look ahead, we want more New Hampshire companies to see UNH as a resource they can turn to for research, equipment, and highly skilled graduates,” said UNH President Elizabeth Chilton. “And we want more students to have the opportunity to apply what they’re learning alongside the businesses that are helping shape the future of this industry.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Janoo leads Scott in final UNH poll; Ayotte tied with Warmington - Yahoo
content: VERMONT (ABC22/FOX44) - A poll conducted mere days before the 2026 general election shows economist Amanda Janoo leading governor Phil Scott. The Green Mountain State Poll, a States of Opinion Project, conducted by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center, puts Janoo up, 51 to 43 percent, with independent Brian Judd taking 4 percent of the vote. A previous poll from the same pollster last month had Janoo up 49 to 43; other polls from Vermont Public and State Navigate, on the other hand, have shown Scott leading Janoo by anywhere between 3 and 10 points. In the Lieutenant Governor's race, the poll by UNH has Molly Gray leading incumbent John Rodgers 63 to 34 percent, and Rep. Becca Balint leading Gerald Malloy 66 to 31 percent. In the Granite State Poll, also conducted by the UNH Survey Center, Governor Kelly Ayotte was tied with former executive councilor Cinde Warmington, 48 to 48 percent. Meanwhile, in the Senate race, one of many that will decide which major party controls Congress in the second half of President Trump's second term, Rep. Chris Pappas now leads former Sen. John Sununu 54 to 42 percent, after narrowly trailing in August. Another result found that most of those voting for Ayotte saw their votes as for her specifically, while most of those voting for Warmington saw themselves as voting for her because she is the Democratic Party nominee. This is the only recent poll, however, that showed such a close race, with other polls last month from Rasmussen, St. Anselm College, and UMass Lowell putting Ayotte ahead by between 6 and 10 points. Democrats in both states, however, viewed the poll with optimism. "New Hampshire voters are ready for change - and they're ready to elect a governor who puts Granite Staters first," said Warmington.
